periods.activity_title: Reading Anand's World of Inventions Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.91): fill missing letters to name inventor qualities.
Let us discuss (p.94): cause-and-effect table for key story events.

homework.task_brief: Let us read (p.91): discuss in groups what the world would be like without inventions.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to name one invention they consider indispensable and say why. Accept brief paired responses to activate thinking about the spirit of curiosity and discovery.

Distribute the word-grid task from “Let us read” (p.91). Students fill in missing letters to reveal the five qualities of an inventor: creativity, curiosity, risk-taking, determination, imagination. Discuss the completed words briefly as a class.

Teacher reads the story aloud, pages 91–98, with students following in their textbooks. Pause twice—once after the burglar-alarm opening and once after the time-machine announcement—for a quick paired prediction exchange before continuing.

Students work on the cause-and-effect table from “Let us discuss” (p.94), tracing four events: the alarm drenching Papa, Anita’s avoidance, watching ‘Back to the Future’, and Papa’s refusal. Pairs share and the class builds a completed table on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The burglar-alarm opening is richly comic—linger there so students register Anita’s dry narrator voice before moving forward. A common difficulty is distinguishing cause from effect in the table; model the first row together before students attempt the rest. The group discussion on a world without inventions is set as an independent task for further reflection.
materials: Blackboard or chart for cause-and-effect table

periods.activity_title: Thinking Deeply: Extracts, Characters, and Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.99): Extract 1 — fill-in, two MCQs, and character comparison.
Let us think and reflect (p.100): character traits table for Anand and Anita.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.101): answer questions 1–5 in writing.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to recall how Anita describes her brother at the start of the story. Invite two or three volunteers to share, anchoring the discussion in the narrator’s amused but affectionate tone.

Work through Extract 1 (“Let us think and reflect,” p.99): students complete the fill-in on what ‘put you in the picture’ means, answer the two MCQs on ‘tinkering’ and Anand’s personality, then write a brief comparison of how Anita and Anand each see him. Discuss answers as a class before moving on.

Students complete the character traits table (p.100), matching traits—creative, curious, careful, responsible, bothersome, confident—to Anand and Anita, each supported by a quoted line from the story. Pairs compare choices; the class settles on the most evidence-backed answers.
Brief oral close: students name one trait from the table they would most like to possess and give a one-sentence reason. This crystallises the character study without requiring written output.

periods.teacher_notes: Extract 1 is the spine of the character-study work—press students to ground every claim in exact words from the text rather than paraphrase. A common pitfall is conflating ‘energetic’ with ‘creative’; the MCQ on personality type is a good moment to address that distinction. Questions 1–5 from ‘Let us think and reflect’ are assigned for independent written practice.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Toby and Speaking the Sounds of –ough

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.105): identify the three true statements from five about Toby.
Let us listen (p.105): fill in exact words from the Anita–Toby conversation.
Let us speak (p.105–106): sort –ough words into pronunciation columns in pairs.

time_bands.activity: Set the scene: Anand’s new project at the story’s end is a telephone to contact outer space. Ask students what they imagine an alien might sound like or say—a quick paired exchange to prime listening attention.

Teacher reads the Anita–Toby conversation aloud at a clear, measured pace (transcript, p.136). Students listen and tick the true statements from the list of five on p.105. After the first reading, students mark choices; teacher reads once more and students confirm or revise.

Teacher reads the transcript a third time, line by line. Students fill in the five blanks on p.105 with the exact words they hear (people, Martians, energy, chocolates, one, clouds, metals). Pairs compare answers before the class checks together.

Move to ‘Let us speak’ (p.105–106). Teacher models the pronunciation of ‘though’ and ‘enough’ from the text, then says each –ough word aloud: bough, dough, through, cough, thought, plough. Pairs sort the words into the five pronunciation columns. Pairs then add at least one more word per column and share with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript hinges on several precise details—Toby misses his ‘people’ (not school), and Anita had an apple (not a banana)—so a second reading is essential before students commit answers. For the speaking task, model each sound column’s key word clearly; students often conflate ‘through’ (/uː/) with ‘thought’ (/ɔː/). Encourage quieter students to read a word aloud during the sorting activity.
materials: Blackboard with five pronunciation column headers

periods.activity_title: Writing About a Vocation with Pride and Purpose

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.106–107): draft a paragraph about a chosen vocation using the given hints.

time_bands.activity: Recall Anand’s obsession with inventing—a passion that mirrors a real vocation. Ask students to call out vocations they know or admire; list six to eight on the board (electrician, chef, nurse, mechanic, graphic designer, etc.) as a shared bank to draw from.

Walk through the seven writing hints on p.106–107 together: why they like the vocation, training needed, tools, co-workers, teamwork, customer dealings, and pursuing it with pride. Model one or two sentences for the vocation ‘nurse’ on the board to show how a hint becomes a sentence.

Students choose their vocation and write their paragraph independently, working through the hints in sequence. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with a question (“What tool does a chef always carry?”) rather than supplying sentences.
Pairs swap paragraphs and read each other’s piece. The reader underlines one sentence they find most convincing and circles one place where more detail would help. Writers revise that section.
Two volunteers read their revised paragraph aloud. The class gives one word of appreciation for each—a brief oral response that closes the writing task with genuine audience engagement.

periods.teacher_notes: Anand’s story frames invention as a vocation pursued with stubborn enthusiasm despite failure—use that spirit to encourage students who struggle to write warmly about their chosen field. A common weakness is listing hints mechanically without connecting them; ask students to aim for two or three sentences that flow naturally from one idea to the next. Both drafting and peer revision happen within this sitting, so the paragraph is complete before students leave.
materials: Lined writing paper or exercise book
Blackboard for shared vocation list and model sentences

periods.activity_title: Language in Action and Exploring Indian Inventors

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.101): match onomatopoeic words to their descriptions.
Let us learn (p.103): identify simple past and past perfect verbs in story sentences.
Let us explore (p.107–108): research an Indian inventor not listed and prepare to share.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.104): fill blanks with simple past or past perfect form of verbs in brackets.

time_bands.activity: Begin with onomatopoeia from ‘Let us learn’ (p.101). Students match crash, humming, hissed, and hammering/sawing/clattering to their descriptions. Discuss how these words make the story’s nighttime scene vivid and tense.

Move to past tense contrast (p.103). Read the two story sentences aloud and ask students to underline verbs in simple past and circle verbs in past perfect. Establish the rule—past perfect marks the earlier of two completed actions—using the story context of Ma discovering Papa drenched and Anand vanishing before dinner.

Introduce ‘Let us explore’ (p.107–108). Students read the four named Indian inventors—Sushruta, Dr. Janaki Ammal, Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, Dr. Narinder Singh Kapany—briefly. Each student then chooses one additional Indian inventor not in the list, notes the invention, and prepares a two-sentence oral share for the class.

Four or five students share their inventor and invention aloud. The class notes any invention they had not heard of before—a quick show of hands closes the exploration with a sense of collective discovery.

periods.teacher_notes: Anchoring the past-perfect rule in the story’s own sentences—Ma rushing in after the alarm soaked Papa—keeps the grammar concrete rather than abstract. Students sometimes use past perfect where simple past is correct; emphasise that past perfect is needed only when two past events must be sequenced. The idiom, binomial, and phrasal-verb tasks from ‘Let us learn’ are rich material for independent study; flag them as self-study reading with references on p.102–103.
materials: Reference books or teacher-provided short notes on Indian inventors

items.source_context: Anand’s burglar alarm, time-machine obsession, Anita’s narrator voice, character traits, and story events.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statement and choose the option that correctly completes it.

Anand’s burglar alarm drenched Papa because ___________.

options.label: A
options.text: Anita accidentally stepped on the alarm wire in the corridor.

options.label: B
options.text: Papa opened the front door softly, triggering the water-bag mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: Papa tried to dismantle the alarm before it was tested.

options.label: D
options.text: The neighbours disturbed the wires while visiting the house.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses Anita’s role; she is the narrator-observer, not the one who triggers the alarm.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student invents a cause not present in the story—no neighbours disturb the wires.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates Papa’s later dismantling of the time machine with the alarm incident.

items.source_context: Anand’s burglar alarm, time-machine obsession, Anita’s narrator voice, character traits, and story events.
items.item_stem: Anita is the narrator of this story, and the reader sees all events through her eyes. What does Anita’s choice to open the story with the burglar-alarm incident reveal about her attitude towards her brother? Use specific details from the story to support your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Anita’s decision to open with the alarm drenching Papa reveals an affectionate but amused detachment; she notes it is ‘not the first time’ Anand has embarrassed the family, suggesting she observes his chaos from a safe distance rather than sharing his excitement. Her dry, matter-of-fact tone shows she is fond of him even while finding him exasperating.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates accurate listening comprehension by identifying true statements and retrieving precise words from a heard conversation.
items.source_context: Anita–Toby conversation: Toby as a Martian stranded on Earth, his abilities, diet, and vision.
items.item_stem: Listen to the conversation between Anita and Toby. Then read the five statements below and decide which are TRUE and which are FALSE. Write TRUE or FALSE for each statement, and for each FALSE statement write a one-sentence correction.

options.text: Anita asks Toby how he can see with only one eye.
Toby misses his people and home on his planet.
Toby says he can see through metals with his eye closed.
Toby says that Martians get their energy from eating fruits.
Toby tells Anita she had a banana for breakfast.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Toby says “I miss my people and home.”
2. False — Toby says Martians get their energy from the Sun, not from eating fruits.
3. True — Anita asks “How are you able to see with only one eye?”
4. False — Toby tells Anita she had an apple (not a banana) for breakfast.
5. True — Toby says “I can see even with my eye closed” and mentions seeing through metals.

items.source_lo: Student demonstrates accurate listening comprehension by identifying true statements and retrieving precise words from a heard conversation.
items.source_context: Anita–Toby conversation: Toby as a Martian stranded on Earth, his abilities, diet, and vision.
items.item_stem: After listening to the conversation between Anita and Toby, answer the following question in 2–3 sentences: Toby tells Anita several things that surprise her. Choose two things Toby reveals about himself and explain why each one would be difficult for a human to imagine.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Toby reveals that Martians do not eat at all and get energy only from the Sun, which is hard for Anita to imagine since she cannot picture life without ice cream and chocolate. He also reveals that he can see through mountains, clouds, wood, and metal even with his eye closed, which no human sense can achieve. These details make Toby feel genuinely alien rather than simply a visitor from another place.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will say each of the following words aloud: bough, dough, through, cough, thought, plough. Say each word aloud after your teacher, then place it in the correct pronunciation column by reading it out in a sentence of your own.

expected_elements: Says each –ough word clearly with the correct vowel sound.
Places every word in the right pronunciation group without hesitation.
Uses the word naturally in a short, meaningful sentence.
Adjusts pronunciation when corrected without repeated prompting.

items.item_stem: Work with a partner. One of you plays the role of Anand explaining his new invention to Anita; the other plays Anita, reacting with surprise or disbelief. In your conversation, include at least four of the following –ough words naturally: though, enough, through, tough, bough, dough. Your teacher will listen for correct pronunciation and natural use.

expected_elements: Uses at least four –ough words with correct pronunciation in context.
Maintains the Anand–Anita sibling dynamic through tone and word choice.
Responds naturally to the partner rather than reciting a rehearsed script.
Self-corrects or requests help when unsure of a pronunciation.

items.item_stem: Choose one of the following vocations: electrician, chef, nurse, or graphic designer. Write a paragraph of 80–100 words that covers: why you find this vocation interesting, what training or skills it requires, and what tools or equipment the work involves. Use the writing hints on p.106–107 of your textbook to organise your paragraph.

expected_elements: States a clear personal reason for choosing the vocation.
Names at least one specific training requirement or skill.
Mentions one or more tools or items of equipment accurately.
Writes in connected sentences with logical order, not a list.

items.source_lo: Student composes a structured paragraph on a real-world vocation, integrating personal choice with practical and thematic detail.
items.source_context: Vocations (electrician, chef, nurse, mechanic, graphic designer); hints on training, tools, teamwork, and pride.
items.item_stem: Anand pursues his passion for inventing with stubborn enthusiasm, even after every failure. Imagine you are advising a younger student who wants to take up any one vocation seriously. Write a short persuasive paragraph (80–100 words) explaining why pride in one’s work and the ability to handle setbacks are essential qualities for success in that vocation. You may draw on the story’s depiction of Anand as well as your own ideas.

expected_elements: Names a specific vocation and links it to pride or perseverance.
Draws a clear connection to Anand’s character or the story’s theme.
Makes a persuasive claim rather than simply describing the vocation.
Uses an appropriate tone for advice directed at a younger student.

items.item_stem: Match each onomatopoeic word from the story with the sound or situation it best describes.
items.visual_stimulus:
Word|Sound or Situation it Describes
Crash|?
Humming|?
Hissed|?
Clattering|?

answer_key.right: A sudden, loud sound of something breaking or colliding
A continuous, low, soothing mechanical sound
Speaking in an angry, sharp whisper
Repeated sharp sounds of hard objects striking each other

items.source_context: Onomatopoeic words (crash, humming, hissed) from the story; simple past and past perfect in sentences featuring Anand, Papa, and Ma.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below describe events from the story. Fill in each blank with the correct form of the verb—simple past or past perfect—to show which action happened first.

(i) By the time Ma __________ (rush) into the room, Papa already __________ (get) soaking wet from the alarm.
(ii) Anand __________ (vanish) from the scene long before Papa __________ (cool) down after dinner.
(iii) After Boppa __________ (enter) Anand’s room, a tremendous crash __________ (echo) through the house.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) rushed / had already got; (ii) had vanished / cooled; (iii) had entered / echoed.

items.item_stem: The textbook ‘Let us explore’ section (p.107–108) mentions four Indian inventors: Sushruta, Dr. Janaki Ammal, Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, and Dr. Narinder Singh Kapany. Choose any one of these inventors. Write four to five sentences explaining who this person was, what they invented or discovered, and why their work matters today.

expected_elements: Names the chosen inventor and their field of work clearly.
States the invention or discovery in specific, accurate terms.
Explains at least one way the invention affects life today.
Writes in coherent sentences with a logical flow of ideas.

items.source_lo: Student investigates and presents information about real-world inventors, connecting the theme of invention to historical and contemporary contexts.
items.source_context: Indian inventors: Sushruta, Dr. Janaki Ammal, Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, Dr. Narinder Singh Kapany; students find additional names.
items.item_stem: Anand in the story is driven by imagination and the refusal to give up, even after every failure. The textbook asks you to find Indian inventors beyond the four listed. Research ONE Indian inventor not mentioned on p.107–108, find out what they invented and what obstacles they faced, and create a short ‘Inventor Profile’: a name card with the inventor’s name, field, key invention, and one sentence on why their story of perseverance matters. Share your profile with the class.

expected_elements: Names an Indian inventor genuinely not listed in the textbook section.
Accurately describes the invention and its significance.
Identifies at least one real obstacle or setback the inventor faced.
Presents the profile clearly enough for classmates to understand without explanation.
